notes: The search still reaches every directive on file, 1940 to last week. What changed is how much of it a mechanic has to read. Every candidate is now weighed against the rule's own applicability wording and put on one of three shelves: the rules that name this product, the rules that turn on what is actually bolted on, and the rules that answer for themselves that this product is not one of theirs. The first shelf is the list you work. The third is folded away with the reason printed on every line, so the answer can be checked instead of trusted. Nothing is dropped — a directive that was found before is still found now.
validated_against: 15 models across Josh's own fleet, against the TBX curated lists: 480 directives on their side, 475 on the first shelf here. The shelf a mechanic works is now the same size as the list he was paying for, with the pre-1994 half TBX's feed cannot reach still in it.
reliability: 40 aircraft configurations searched end to end: 0 page errors, 0 problems. Full entries to read across the 40 fell from 3,794 to 2,042, with 1,752 kept as one-line rows that open on a tap. The 12 MB index has moved out of the inspection database into the service worker's cache — verified offline with the network switched off: 0 network requests, search still returns.

index.source: FAA Dynamic Regulatory System, AD Final Rules

fix: A family rule of mine was treating an enumeration of sibling models as a claim on the whole family. A PA-28-181 Archer was being handed 79 directives when the aeroplane has about 31 — 43 of them were rules about a Cherokee 140, an Arrow, or a Warrior. Two causes: the index builder plucked "PA-28" out of the middle of "PA-28-140" and filed it as a family, and the prefix rule read a sibling as a parent. Both fixed, and every family match is now graded against the rule's own words before it is shown. Where a bare designation is itself a real model — Mooney's M20 — a rule that lists M20, M20A, M20B is read as an enumeration, not a family claim.
storage: The directive index no longer shares a database with jobs and photographs. It lives in Cache Storage under 'adx-1'. Any copy left in the old place is deleted on first load. This is the second half of the 30 August fix: the database that wedged that morning is now smaller and is never touched by an AD search.
